P1_fx_receipts.question: Can resident individuals receive foreign currency for services or digital exports? Any conversion or repatriation rule?
P1_fx_receipts.answer: Yes, through Ethiopian banks, within NBE controls. Since the February 2026 relaxation of Directive FXD/01/2024 (amendment FXD/04/2026), any service exporter may keep 100% of export proceeds in a foreign-exchange retention account indefinitely. Previously part had to be converted. Goods exporters still face a 50% conversion rule. Retention-account holders can get internationally recognised cards for outbound e-commerce payments. Whether an unregistered individual freelancer counts as a 'service exporter' eligible for a retention account was not established; banks may require a TIN and business licence.

sources.title: Public Notice: Relaxation of Foreign Exchange Directives (FXD/01/2024), Feb 2026
sources.quote: Any service exporter is allowed to hold one hundred percent (100%) of its export proceeds in foreign exchange retention account for indefinite periods.

sources.title: Public Notice — cards for FX account holders
sources.quote: Authorized banks are allowed to issue internationally recognized cards for all foreign exchange account holders that will be used by the customers to make outbound retail payments including e-commerce as long as the account holders have sufficient FX in their accounts.

sources.title: NBE rolls out major forex liberalization: 100% Retention for Service Exporters (11 Feb 2026)
sources.quote: Service exporters will now be allowed to retain 100 percent of their export proceeds in foreign exchange retention accounts for an indefinite period, a significant shift from previous retention limits and time caps.

P1_fx_receipts.notes: The directive PDF (FXD/04/2026) link on nbe.gov.et returned 404; the NBE public notice was read. Tech-ish (secondary) frames it as covering freelance developers, but the NBE text says 'service exporter' without defining individuals.

P2_fcy_account.question: Can resident individuals hold a foreign-currency account locally?
P2_fcy_account.answer: Yes, for qualifying sources. Service exporters use retention accounts (P1). The February 2026 relaxation also removed the USD 100 minimum for foreign-exchange savings accounts for resident and non-resident Ethiopians. FX account holders may pay a spouse's and children's education, medical and travel costs abroad from the account with documents.

sources.title: Public Notice — FX savings accounts
sources.quote: The minimum requirement, USD 100 to open a foreign exchange savings account for resident and non-resident Ethiopians, including foreign nationals of Ethiopian origin has been removed.

sources.title: Public Notice — uses of FX accounts
sources.quote: Any foreign exchange account holder, including retention accounts holders, can pay from his/her forex account for his/her spouse’s and children’s education, medical and travel expenses abroad upon presentation of valid documents.

P2_fcy_account.notes: Which inflows a resident's ordinary FX savings account may receive (beyond retention-account export proceeds) was not established from the directive text.

P3_local_gateways.question: Which local payment gateways can an individual or sole trader use to accept online payments?
P3_local_gateways.answer: Global platform availability for Ethiopia (automated collector snapshots, Oct 2026). Available: Paddle (not on its exclusion list; software sellers only, each seller reviewed); Lemon Squeezy (bank payouts); Polar (payouts); Whop (payouts); Dodo Payments (sellers); Google Play (developer registration). Not listed: Stripe (merchant sign-up); Etsy seller payments; YouTube Partner Program.

P3_local_gateways.notes: Chapa, NBE-licensed in 2022 and the first non-bank payment gateway, lets businesses accept local and international payment methods. Merchant onboarding requirements could not be read from Chapa's own site (client-side rendering); press reports describe KYC with business details. Sources are from 2022. Whether an unlicensed individual can onboard (vs. a TIN plus business licence) is unconfirmed. Telebirr merchant options not researched.

P4_paypal.question: Can residents receive money via PayPal?
P4_paypal.answer: No. Ethiopia is a listed PayPal market, but Ethiopian-registered accounts can only send and shop. They cannot receive payments or withdraw to Ethiopian banks. Ethiopia is not on the PayPal Payouts list. Xoom (PayPal-owned) handles inbound remittances to Ethiopia, which is a separate service.

P4_paypal.notes: Accounts 'linked to international accounts' (registered abroad) are not a lawful route for residents, and the guide does not recommend them.

P5_payoneer_wise.question: Payoneer / Wise availability for residents
P5_payoneer_wise.answer: Wise: Ethiopia is NOT on Wise's list of countries whose residents can hold money. Payoneer: no reliable source confirming Payoneer accounts and withdrawals to Ethiopian banks for residents was found. A 2026 guide mentions Payoneer use only loosely. Proceeds should reach an Ethiopian bank, where service-export receipts can sit in a retention account (P1).

L1_registration.question: Must an individual register a business to sell digital services/products? Simplest legal form?
L1_registration.answer: A formal sole proprietorship means commercial registration (unique trade name) and a business licence from the Ministry of Trade and regional trade bureaus, increasingly online via the eTrade portal, with a TIN. In practice, tax rules penalise unlicensed suppliers: payers withhold 30% instead of 3% when the supplier has no TIN and business licence. Informal individual online sellers are still 'E-Commerce Operators' under the e-commerce law.

L2_tax_id.question: Tax ID: who needs one, how to get it?
L2_tax_id.answer: The TIN from the Ministry of Revenues. Since late 2023 tax registration has been linked to the Fayda national digital ID, so a Fayda number is effectively required. Fayda is legal and sufficient proof of identity and is used to obtain business licences.

L3_income_tax_foreign.question: Income tax on foreign-source income for residents; rates or special regimes
L3_income_tax_foreign.answer: Resident individuals are taxed on worldwide income. Under Income Tax (Amendment) Proclamation 1395/2025 (in effect from July 2025), individual business income is taxed 0% up to ETB 24,000, then 15%, 20%, 25%, 30%, and 35% above ETB 168,000. Individuals with turnover under ETB 2m (Category B) pay tax on gross sales at 2–9%, but professional service providers (accounting, architectural, consulting, legal, etc.) may not use gross-sales taxation. Digital content creators' income is business income if earned regularly for profit; otherwise it is taxed at 15% as other income.

L4_vat_gst.question: VAT/GST: rate, registration threshold, treatment of exported digital services
L4_vat_gst.answer: VAT Proclamation 1341/2024: the standard rate is 15%, and registration is required at ETB 2m of taxable supplies in 12 months. Exports of goods and services are zero-rated where the proclamation's zero-rating conditions are met.

L5_data_protection.question: Data-protection law applicable to a small online business
L5_data_protection.answer: Personal Data Protection Proclamation 1321/2024: to process personal data, a data controller or processor must be registered with the Authority, the Ethiopian Communications Authority (art. 33). The Authority may set registration requirements by directive. No small-business exemption was found.

L6_consumer_ecommerce.question: Consumer-protection / e-commerce rules for online sales (refunds, disclosures)
L6_consumer_ecommerce.answer: Electronic Transaction Proclamation 1205/2020: sellers must disclose business details and transaction conditions. Per commentary on the law, a consumer may return goods or services without cause within 7 days of receipt for a full refund (consumer pays return costs). If the information duties are not met, the consumer may withdraw within 14 days of receipt.

L7_incentives.question: Legal incentives / tax holidays / special zones relevant to small digital businesses
L7_incentives.answer: (1) 100% FX retention for service exporters, indefinitely, since February 2026 (P1). (2) Gross-sales tax of 2–9% for individuals under ETB 2m turnover, except professional services (L3). (3) Zero-rated VAT on qualifying exports (L4). (4) No USD minimum to open an FX savings account (P2).

W1_workarounds.question: Simple, legal routes around payment barriers for a beginner (no misrepresentation, nominees or sanctions evasion)
W1_workarounds.answer: Barriers: Stripe does not accept merchants here; platforms that pay out through PayPal Payouts cannot pay PayPal accounts here (not on PayPal's Payouts list, see P4 for ordinary PayPal receiving); Wise does not let residents hold money. Simple legal routes: (1) Sell digital products or software through a merchant of record: Paddle (software/SaaS only; each seller reviewed), Lemon Squeezy (bank payouts), Polar, Dodo Payments. The platform is the legal seller to your customers, handles card payments and consumer VAT/sales tax, and pays you out. You still declare the payouts as your income at home (see L3). (2) Sell services on Upwork, which is available here (not on its restricted list). Which withdrawal methods you get (bank, PayPal, Payoneer, etc.) depends on the country and shows in your account. (3) For direct clients, a bank transfer (SWIFT) into your own local account always works. Follow the local foreign-exchange rules (see P1) and keep invoices. (4) Local official channel: Since February 2026, service exporters may keep 100% of export proceeds in a foreign-exchange retention account (NBE directive) (P1/P2). Avoid: opening accounts with a foreign address, a relative's or friend's identity, or a VPN to look like you are elsewhere. It breaches platform terms (accounts and funds get frozen) and can break anti-money-laundering or sanctions law.
